chunks: From him, from Abu Abdillah, from Al-Hasan ibn Zadif, from Ibn Abi Umayr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who has wealth belonging to orphans in his possession, and he does not pay it to them until they die, then their heir or their agent comes to him and makes a settlement with him that he should waive part of it and take part of it, and be acquitted of what was upon him; is he acquitted from it? He said, 'Yes.'

And about a man who has wealth belonging to another man in his possession, either from a sale or a loan, and he dies without having paid it to him, leaving behind young orphans, so it remains due from him to them and he does not pay it to them; is he among those who consume the wealth of the orphans unjustly? He said, 'No, if he intended to pay it to them.'

key_terms.يَأْكُلُ أَمْوَالَ الْيَتَامَى ظُلْمًا: Consuming the wealth of orphans unjustly

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on a trustee who holds orphans' wealth and settles with their heir before paying the full amount?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam* clarifies the legal nuances of debt settlement involving orphans, distinguishing between the validity of pre-death compromise (*sulh*) and the posthumous status of the debtor. It highlights the Shia scholarly emphasis on *niyyah* (intention) as a mitigating factor for 'consuming wealth unjustly' (*akl al-mal bi-l-batil*), ensuring that a debtor who dies owing orphans is not penalized if he intended to fulfill the obligation.
